## Structures of Economic Data
\begin{itemize}
  \item Just like Economics is classified into Macro and Micro, we divide data/econometrics in the same way:

  \vspace{0.2cm}

  \item \textbf{Micro-econometric data} :
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Cross-sectional data
    \item Pooled/repeated cross sections
    \item Panel or longitudinal data (e.g.\ CK \& S)
  \end{itemize}

  \vspace{0.2cm}

  \item \textbf{Macro-econometric data} :
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Cross-sectional data
    \item Time series data
    \item Macro panel data
  \end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\textcolor{red}{The unit-of-observation is very important.}

## Micro-econometric Data

\begin{itemize}
  \item Consist of samples of individuals, households, firms, or other micro-level units. Observations refer to micro-economic units; widely used in development economics, labour economics, and industrial organisation.
  \item Commonly used to test microeconomic hypotheses and evaluate economic policies.
  \item Typically collected through: Surveys, Administrative databases, Web-scraped data. Ideally obtained using random sampling methods.
  
  \item Observed either:
  \begin{itemize}
    \item At a single point in time: \textbf{cross-sectional data},
    \item Over multiple time periods (usually a few years): 
    	\begin{itemize}
		\item When the \textcolor{blue}{same} micro-units are followed over time: \textbf{panel data}
		\item When different samples are observed over time: \textbf{repeated cross-sections}	
	\end{itemize}
  \end{itemize}
  
  \item Dummy variables and categorical variables are commonly used.
  
\end{itemize}

## Example: US Gun Policy Dataset

\begin{itemize}
  \item The \textcolor{blue}{US Gun Policy dataset} from Siegel et al.\ (2019). The dataset contains:
  \begin{itemize}
    \item 51 states, indexed by $s$,
    \item 21 years, indexed by $t$ (2001--2021),
    \item A total of $1{,}071$ state--year ($st$) observations,
    \item A unit of observation defined as a \underline{state--year}.\\
 \textbf{This is an example of an aggregated (balanced) panel dataset. }
   
  \end{itemize}

  \item The \textcolor{blue}{Card--Krueger dataset} is a micro-level (balanced) panel: Two observations for each of 410 fast-food outlets.

  \item The \textcolor{blue}{BHPS/US dataset}(next example): Household-level panel dataset.

\end{itemize}

## UK Datasets

Examples of well-used publicly available datasets:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textcolor{blue}{FES}  Family Expenditure Survey; Annual survey; About 30,000 different households each year.
  \item \textcolor{blue}{CP} Census of Production; Annual survey; Sample of firms aggregated to 4-digit (225) industries.

  \item \textcolor{blue}{BHPS/US}  British Household Panel Survey; Annual survey; About 10,000 households each year since 1991;The same households are interviewed every year; Since 2009/10 it has been called \textit{Understanding Society}.

  \item \textcolor{blue}{LFS}  Labour Force Survey; Quarterly rolling panel; About 55,000 households; Each household is interviewed for five consecutive quarters and then dropped.
\end{itemize}
\vspace{0.3cm}
Much better to look at \textcolor{blue}{The UK Data Archive}.

## Econometrics so far

\begin{itemize}
  \item Simple regression:
  \[
  y = \alpha + \beta x + u.
  \]

  \item The key issue is whether or not the \underline{exogeneity assumption}  holds
  \[
  E(u \mid x) \equiv E(ux) = \text{Cov}(u,x) = 0 \tag{A2}
  \]
 \item Even though OLS \underline{by construction} imposes the sample analogue:
  \[
  \sum_i \hat{u}_i x_i = 0.
  \]
\end{itemize}
\textit{Reference: Lecture notes - Introduction }

## Econometrics so far
\begin{itemize}
  \item Given (A2), the OLS estimator for $\beta$ is:
  \[
  \hat{\beta}
  = \frac{\widehat{\text{Cov}}(y,x)}{\widehat{\text{Var}}(x)}
  = \frac{\sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})(x_i - \bar{x})}
         {\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}.
  \]

  \item The data \underline{cannot} help us decide whether (A2) is true, since $u$ is unobserved.

  \item If (A2) is true, we can talk about \textbf{causal effects} and OLS being an \textbf{unbiased estimator}.

  \item Hypothesis testing was covered twice:
  \[
  H_0 : \beta = 0 
  \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  H_0 : \mu_1 = \mu_2.
  \]
\end{itemize}

## Example 1

\begin{block}{\textbf{Are Danes the happiest nation in the world?}}
This ``stylised fact'' is well known, and Danes are often thought to be happier than their neighbours, the Swedes.
\end{block}

\vspace{0.3cm}

You can test this Danes vs.\ Swedes comparison using methods from Lecture 2:

\[
H_0 : \mu_1 = \mu_2 
\qquad \text{and} \qquad 
H_a : \mu_1 \neq \mu_2,
\]
using $\bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_2$ to construct a test statistic.

## Example 2
\begin{block}{\textbf{Pfizer--BioNTech Vaccine Efficacy}}
For microeconomists, the Random Control Trial (RCT) is the gold standard in causal inference.  
Sometimes, RCTs are important globally. The results of the first Pfizer--BioNTech clinical trial
(published December 2020) are:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\hline
 & Pfizer--BioNTech & Placebo injection \\
\hline
Number in each group        & 18,198 & 18,325 \\
Number of Covid-19 cases   & 8      & 162    \\
Proportion getting the disease & 0.043\% & 0.884\% \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\vspace{0.3cm}
The vaccine \textbf{efficacy} is 95\%.
\end{block}


## Example 2

\begin{itemize}
  \item Taken from Table 22.1 in \textit{Covid by Numbers}.  
  Do not read the original article (in the \textit{New England Journal of Medicine}).

  \item Efficacy is defined as:
  \[
  E = 1 - \frac{\mu_T}{\mu_C}
    = \frac{\mu_C - \mu_T}{\mu_C}.
  \]

  \item This is a \textbf{normalised difference in probabilities}.

  \item When $\mu_T = 0$ (none of the treated are ill), then $E = 1$ (total efficacy).

  \item When $\mu_C = \mu_T$, then $E = 0$ (the vaccine has no effect).

  \item \textbf{Vaccine efficacy} is the correct terminology  
  (and is not the same as vaccine \textbf{effectiveness}).

  \item Population probabilities $\mu$ are estimated by sample proportions $p$.
\end{itemize}


## Example 2

\begin{itemize}
  \item The underlying individual variable $y_i$ is binary:
  \[
  y_i = 
  \begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if the outcome is true (here: gets Covid)},\\
  0 & \text{otherwise.}
  \end{cases}
  \]

  \item The reported statistics are sample means, i.e.\ the proportion of (sub)samples for which $y=1$:
  \(
  p = \bar{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i y_i.
  \)

  \item The data can be summarised by a \textbf{cross tabulation}:
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.3cm}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{l|cc|c}
 & \textbf{Covid} & \textbf{Not Covid} &  \\
  & $(y_i=1)$ &  $(y_i=0)$ &  \\
\hline
Treated $(d_i=1)$  & $n_{11}$ & $n_{01}$ & 
$p_T = n_{11}/(n_{11}+n_{01})$ \\[0.2cm]
Control $(d_i=0)$  & $n_{10}$ & $n_{00}$ & 
$p_C = n_{10}/(n_{10}+n_{00})$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

## Example 2
\begin{itemize}
  \item In the trial,
  \[
  n_{11} = 8, 
  \quad n_{10} = 168, 
  \quad n_{11} + n_{01} = 18{,}198, 
  \quad n_{10} + n_{00} = 18{,}325,
  \]
  and the estimated efficacy is calculated as:
  \[
  \hat{E}
  = 1 - \frac{p_T}{p_C}
  = \frac{p_C - p_T}{p_C}
  = 1 - \frac{0.00043}{0.00884}
  = 0.95.
  \]

  \item The reported 95\% confidence interval is $(0.90,\,0.98)$.  
  (Do not worry about how this is calculated.)
\end{itemize}

## Example 3
\begin{block}{\textbf{How much should tuition fees be?}}
In the early 2000s, the claim was that graduates, on average, earn more than \pounds 400{,}000 more than non-graduates over their lifetime.  
This argument was used by the Government at the time to increase tuition fees to \pounds 3{,}200 per year in 2006.  
After that, fees increased to \pounds 9{,}000 per year following the October 2010 Spending Review (and are now \pounds 9{,}250 per year).
\end{block}

\vspace{0.4cm}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \pounds 400{,}000 is only an average and varies by subject, occupation, and other characteristics.
  \item More generally, what is the return to investment in education (schooling)? 5\% per annum? 10\% per annum?
  
\end{itemize}

## Example 5

\begin{block}{\textbf{August babies flop at exams}}
``Amongst girls born in September, 60.7\% achieve at least five A* to C grade GCSEs, 
compared with only 55.2\% for those born in August'' (IFS).  

The corresponding figures for boys are 50.3\% and 44.2\%.
\end{block}

\vspace{0.15cm}
Is this August/September difference statistically significant?  
What information do we need in order to carry out a formal test?

\vspace{0.4cm}

A similar US variation in educational achievement by month of birth was exploited in a famous paper by 
Joshua Angrist (from the textbook \textit{Mastering ’Metrics}) and Alan Krueger (already seen in Lecture~1).  
Angrist shared half of the 2021 Nobel Prize for this paper and related work.  
See \textit{Mastering ’Metrics}, Section~6.3.


## Example 6

\begin{block}{\textbf{Did the Education Maintenance Allowance (EMA) improve staying-on rates?}}
In England, between 2004 and 2010, a young person was eligible to receive an allowance of up to \pounds 30 per week provided they stayed on at school and their parents earned less than \pounds 30{,}000 per year.  
The aim of the programme was to encourage more young people to stay on in education.
\end{block}

\vspace{0.15cm}

From the \textit{Longitudinal Survey of Young People in England}, 5,011 young persons were observed in Year~11:

\begin{itemize}
  \item 2,393 were eligible, of whom 58.1\% stayed on.
  \item 2,618 were ineligible, of whom 63.4\% stayed on.
\end{itemize}

The raw differential is $-5.3$ percentage points, and so the policy appears \underline{not} to have worked.

Can we use the same Difference-in-Differences (DiD) methodology as introduced in Lecture 1 and developed more formally in Lecture 7?


## Raw Differentials
\begin{itemize}
  \item Every week we see evidence like this being reported, mainly coming from micro-econometric data.
  \vspace{-0.05cm}
  \item Although we are interested in raw averages themselves, more often we want to compare averages across categories:
  \begin{itemize}
  \vspace{-0.1cm}
    \item Danes vs.\ Swedes
     \vspace{-0.1cm}
    \item Treated vs.\ control
    \vspace{-0.1cm}
    \item Boys vs.\ girls
    \vspace{-0.1cm}
    \item (Not) affected by the NMW
    \vspace{-0.1cm}
    \item (In)eligible for EMA
    \vspace{-0.1cm}
  \end{itemize}
   \vspace{-0.05cm}
  \item These comparisons are called \textbf{raw differentials}.
 
  \item Regression handles this naturally: the RHS variable $x$ becomes a \textbf{dummy variable}.
  \item Differences in raw differentials are also very common and are known as 
  \textbf{differences-in-differences} (or \textbf{diff-in-diffs}, DiDs).
\end{itemize}

## Simple Regression when x is a Dummy
\begin{itemize}
    \item We start with the same model,
    \[
    y = \alpha + \beta x + u, \qquad x \in \{0,1\}, \tag{1}
    \]
    but now \(x\) is either 0 (e.g.\ a woman) or 1 (e.g.\ a man).
    \item \(x\) is said to be a dummy variable. There are many of these variables in cross-section datasets.
\end{itemize}

## Simple Regression when x is a Dummy
\begin{figure}[htbp]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.7\textwidth]{/Users/gitrepos/ECON20222/images/simplereg_dummy.png}
\end{figure}


## Simple Regression when x is a Dummy
\begin{itemize}
    \item To estimate the two parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), we require two moment conditions (exogeneity assumptions):
    \begin{equation}
        E(u \mid x = 0) = E(u \mid x = 1) = 0. \tag{A3}
    \end{equation}
    \item Write the population regression function for the cases \(x = 0\) and \(x = 1\), and take conditional expectations:
    \begin{align}
        \mu_2 &\equiv E(y \mid x = 0) 
        = \alpha + E(u \mid x = 0), \tag{2} \\
        \mu_1 &\equiv E(y \mid x = 1) 
        = \alpha + \beta + E(u \mid x = 1). \tag{3}
    \end{align}
    \item Imposing Assumption (A3) yields:
    \[
        E(y \mid x = 0) = \alpha + 0, 
        \qquad 
        E(y \mid x = 1) = \alpha + \beta + 0.
    \]
    \item Consequently,
    \begin{equation}
        \beta 
        = E(y \mid x = 1) - E(y \mid x = 0)
        = \mu_1 - \mu_2. \tag{4}
    \end{equation}
\end{itemize}
\noindent
Thus, \(\beta\) - \textbf{population raw differential}

## Simple Regression when x is a Dummy
\begin{itemize}
    \item Replacing population means by their sample averages, the OLS estimator is given by
    \begin{equation}
        \hat{\beta} = \bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_2, \tag{5}
    \end{equation}
    which is the \textbf{sample raw differential}. Moreover, \(\hat{\alpha} = \bar{y}_2\).
    \item The fitted regression line \(\hat{\alpha} + \hat{\beta} x_i\) can be written as
    \begin{equation}
        \hat{y}_i = \bar{y}_2 + (\bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_2)x_i. \tag{6}
    \end{equation}
    \item The residual is defined as \(\hat{u}_i \equiv y_i - \hat{y}_i\). Hence,
    \[
        \hat{u}_i =
        \begin{cases}
            y_i - \bar{y}_2, & \text{if } x_i = 0; \\[0.5em]
            y_i - \bar{y}_1, & \text{if } x_i = 1.
        \end{cases}
    \]
\end{itemize}

## Simple Regression when x is a Dummy
Hypothesis test: To examine whether the population means of the two sub-samples are equal:
    \[
        H_0 : \mu_1 = \mu_2 
        \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad 
       H_0 : \beta = 0.
    \]
  \begin{itemize} 
    \item The test statistic is given by \(\hat{\beta}/\mathrm{se}(\hat{\beta})\), which turns out to be exactly the same as
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{\bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_2}
        {\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{\sigma}_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{\hat{\sigma}_2^2}{n_2}}}. \tag{7}
    \end{equation}
    This is a very well-known formula.
    \item One might ask why we need to estimate a regression model when it suffices to compute the two sample means and their variances to obtain the same result. The reason is that regression analysis provides a unified and general framework that encompasses a wide range of econometric models and hypothesis tests.
\end{itemize}

## Simple Regression when x is a Dummy
\begin{itemize}
    \item When the dependent variable is in logarithmic form,
    \[
        \log y = \alpha + \beta x + u,
    \]
    then equation (5) becomes
    \[
        \hat{\beta} = \log \bar{y}_1 - \log \bar{y}_2.
    \]
    \item The following algebra provides a unit-free interpretation:
    \begin{align*}
        \hat{\beta}
        &= \log \bar{y}_1 - \log \bar{y}_2 \\
        &= \log \left( 1 + \frac{\bar{y}_1 - \bar{y}_2}{\bar{y}_2} \right) \\
        &\equiv \log \left( 1 + \frac{\%\Delta y}{100} \right) \\
        &\approx \frac{\%\Delta y}{100}, \qquad \text{if } \frac{\%\Delta y}{100} \text{ is small.}
    \end{align*}
    \item Why does this approximation hold? 
    \(\log(1 + x) \approx x \quad \text{for small } x  \; (\text{e.g., } |x| < 0.1). \)
\end{itemize}

## Simple Regression when x is a Dummy
\begin{itemize}
    \item when \(\%\Delta y / 100\) is small, one can interpret \(\hat{\beta}\) as the raw differential in the dependent variable. This is typically described as a \textbf{log-point change}.
    \item When \(\%\Delta y / 100\) is \underline{not} small, the same concept must be computed from the third line:
    \[
        \%\Delta y = 100\,[\exp(\hat{\beta}) - 1],
    \]
    which is described as a \textbf{percentage-point raw differential}.
\end{itemize}

## BHPS/US Example
\begin{itemize}
    \item Formerly known as the British Household Panel Survey (BHPS).
    \item The BHPS/US is particularly well suited for studying differences between individuals since, by design, it records a rich set of information on people’s lives.
    \item We will examine an extract from the data in order to replicate some of the examples discussed above.
    \item We will later show why panel data are superior to repeated cross-sections.
    \item The 14 variables that have been extracted correspond to 58{,}640 individuals \(i\), who are observed one, two, or three times across waves \(t = 1, 2, 3\).
\end{itemize}

## BHPS/US Example
\begin{itemize}
    \item In \texttt{20222\_USoc\_extract.dta}, about half of the sample (59{,}216 observations) are in paid employment. 
    Their ages vary substantially, and therefore they also differ considerably in their years of work experience, among other characteristics.
    \item When we take logs of real hourly pay and regress on a male dummy variable, we obtain an estimate of 0.183(0.0051). This says, on average earn\(0.183\) log-points more than females which converts to 20.1\%.
    \item A large proportion of individuals do not hold a university degree (102{,}644 observations), while the remainder do (30{,}397 observations). (Note the recoding of the degree variable.) When we regress log real hourly pay on a degree dummy variable, we obtain
0.472 (0.0051), which corresponds to 60.3\%.
    \item This represents a very large raw differential. What is its implication over a lifetime? 
\end{itemize}

## Outlook
Next week: Lecture 4 Endogeneity, Lecture 5 Multiple regression
\begin{itemize}
    \item In multiple regression, one can run both regressions simultaneously; that is, more than one right-hand-side (RHS) variable (in addition to the constant) can be included. One typically obtains similar, though not identical, estimates and standard errors.
    \item There are additional variables in \texttt{20222\_USoc\_extract.dta} relating to individuals’ ethnicity, place of residence, and the size of the firm that employs them. These are multi-category dummy variables. Multiple regression applies in this context as well, although some recoding is required beforehand.
    \item The differences-in-differences methodology can also be implemented using multiple regression (covered in Lecture~7).
    \item Indeed, multiple regression is the workhorse technique in almost all of microeconometrics.
\end{itemize}
